Hello, I'm Ji-woo, and I'm one of the organisers of the Hillside Night Ride, a twenty-kilometre bike ride through the city after dark. Thank you for coming to this briefing.

The ride starts at nine p.m. from the university car park. We originally planned to start at eight, but sunset is quite late at this time of year, and we wanted it to be properly dark so you can enjoy the lights. You should arrive at least half an hour before the start to check in.

This isn't a race. It's a slow, social ride, and we'll travel at about fifteen kilometres per hour. Leaders in orange jackets will ride at the front, and helpers in yellow jackets will be at the back to make sure nobody gets left behind.

Lights are essential. You must have a white light on the front and a red light on the back. We'll also be giving everyone some glow sticks to decorate their bikes. In fact, there's a prize for the best-decorated bike, which will be judged at the halfway point, in Victoria Gardens.

At Victoria Gardens, there'll be a twenty-minute break with hot drinks. Local residents have kindly agreed to provide homemade cakes, but please pay what you can, as the money goes to the gardens' maintenance fund.

The route ends back at the university at around half past eleven. If you don't feel able to finish, there's a shortcut back from Victoria Gardens, which takes about fifteen minutes.

Children can take part if they're over twelve and riding with an adult. Younger children can ride in a trailer or child seat.

Finally, please remember that some roads are not completely closed to traffic, so stay on the left and follow instructions from the marshals.

[Notes]
Leaders wear (4) ______ jackets
Prize for: best-decorated (5) ______
question: Why was the start time changed?
choices: to make sure it is fully dark
to avoid heavy traffic
to give riders more time to check in
answer: to make sure it is fully dark
explanation: 日没が遅いので、明かりを楽しめるよう完全に暗くなる9時に変更した。

And now on Radio Westvale, our weekly look at what's on locally. This week, it's all about the new farmers' market in Linton.

The market started in April and takes place on the second and fourth Saturday of every month. It's held in the car park of Linton Primary School, which is closed at weekends. Originally, the organisers wanted to use the high street, but the council said closing the road would cause too many traffic problems.

There are around thirty stalls, and every one of them sells food that has been grown or produced within thirty miles of the town. That's the main rule of the market. You'll find vegetables, cheese, eggs, bread and honey, as well as a few stalls selling plants and flowers.

I spoke to one of the organisers, Grace Mensah, who said the market's aim isn't just to sell food. They also want to bring the community together. For example, there's a cooking demonstration every market day at eleven, where a local chef shows people how to cook with whatever's in season. Last week it was asparagus soup.

The market has introduced a scheme to reduce waste. If you bring your own bags and containers, you'll get a stamp on a loyalty card. Collect ten stamps, and you get a five-pound voucher to spend at any stall.

Most stalls accept cards, but not all, so it's a good idea to bring some cash. There's no cash machine nearby.

And for anyone with young children, there's a craft table run by volunteers, so parents can shop in peace.

The market runs from nine until one. The next one is this Saturday.

[Notes]
Loyalty card: 10 stamps = £5 (4) ______
Advice: bring some (5) ______ (no cash machine)
question: Why is the market not held on the high street?
choices: Closing the road would cause traffic problems.
The shops on the high street objected.
There was not enough space for the stalls.
answer: Closing the road would cause traffic problems.
explanation: 主催者は大通りを使いたかったが、道を閉じると交通問題になると議会に言われた。

Good morning, and welcome to this information meeting for new stallholders at the Riverside Farmers' Market. I'm Tobias, the market manager, and I'll explain the main things you need to know.

First, setting up. Vehicles can enter the market square from six a.m., and all vehicles must be moved to the back car park by 7.45, because the market opens to the public at eight. Last year we allowed vans to stay behind the stalls, but customers complained that the fumes and noise spoilt the atmosphere, so that's no longer permitted.

Stall fees are thirty pounds per market day. You can pay monthly or for the whole season. If you pay for the season in advance, you'll save about fifteen percent, and you'll be guaranteed the same pitch each week, which regular customers find helpful.

All food must be clearly labelled. Labels must show the name of the farm or producer and a list of ingredients for anything that's been prepared, like jams or pies. Allergy information is particularly important; please make sure nuts and dairy products are clearly marked.

We are trying to become plastic-free by next year. That means no plastic bags at all. Paper bags are fine, and we have a supplier who offers stallholders a discount.

Now, a word about the weather. The market goes ahead in all conditions except very strong winds. If we have to cancel, we'll send a text message by six a.m. You won't be charged for cancelled days.

Finally, every stallholder is expected to help out with one community event during the year, such as the harvest festival in September. Details of these will be emailed to you in a newsletter.

[Notes]
Labels must show: producer's name and list of (4) ______
Cancellation notice sent by (5) ______ message
question: Why can vans no longer stay behind the stalls?
choices: Customers disliked the noise and fumes.
There was not enough space for them.
The council changed the parking rules.
answer: Customers disliked the noise and fumes.
explanation: 排気ガスと騒音で雰囲気が悪くなるという苦情があったため。

Hello everyone. My name's Lucia, and I'm the volunteer coordinator for the Greenford Farmers' Market. Thank you so much for offering to help out. I'll explain the different jobs, and then you can choose which ones you'd like to do.

The first job is setting up the information tent. This involves putting up the tent, arranging leaflets and maps, and then answering questions from visitors. It's a great job if you like talking to people. We need two people for this every week.

Then there's the recycling team. They walk around the market emptying bins and making sure food waste goes into the compost bins. It's quite physical, so we usually ask younger volunteers to do this, but anyone who's fit is welcome.

We also need someone to help with our social media. This used to be done by a professional, but we've decided to use volunteers instead, so we can spend the money on advertising in the local paper. You'd need to take photos of the stalls and post them during the market.

Another important job is the "Taste of the Season" stall. Here, volunteers give out free samples of fruit and vegetables that farmers donate. It's very popular with children, and it helps people try things they've never eaten before.

All volunteers get a free coffee and a ten percent discount at most stalls. And at the end of the season, we hold a thank-you dinner for everyone.

Volunteers need to arrive by half past seven on market days, and you can leave at one, after we've packed up. You'll need to wear the green apron we'll give you today, so people can recognise you.

Now, does anyone have any questions?

[Notes]
"Taste of the Season" stall: free (4) ______ of fruit and vegetables
Volunteers must wear: green (5) ______
question: Which job is recommended for people who enjoy talking to others?
choices: working in the information tent
joining the recycling team
taking photos and posting them on social media
explanation: 人と話すのが好きなら information tent の仕事がよいと言っている。

The first job is setting up the information tent. This involves putting up the tent, arranging leaflets and maps, and then answering questions from visitors. It's a great job if you like talking to people. We need two people for this every week.

All volunteers get a free coffee and a ten percent discount at most stalls. And at the end of the season, we hold a thank-you dinner for everyone.

Volunteers need to arrive by half past seven on market days, and you can leave at one, after we've packed up. You'll need to wear the green apron we'll give you today, so people can recognise you.

Now, does anyone have any questions?

passage:
Good morning, ladies and gentlemen, and welcome aboard the Dale Valley Heritage Railway. My name is Arthur, and I'll be your guide on today's journey from Kirkby Station to Ravensdale.

This line was first opened in 1868 to carry stone from the quarries in the hills. Passenger trains were added later, but the line closed completely in 1962, when lorries took over the stone traffic. In 1985, a group of volunteers started to restore it, and the first heritage train ran again in 1994. Today, the railway is still run almost entirely by volunteers. There are only six paid staff.

The engine pulling us today is called Morning Star. It was built in 1921, and it spent thirty years in a museum before it was repaired. It uses about a tonne of coal on each round trip.

The journey to Ravensdale takes about fifty minutes. About halfway, we'll cross the Hallam Viaduct, which is twenty-eight metres high. You'll get the best view from the right-hand side of the train.

At Ravensdale, you'll have an hour and a half before the return journey. There's a small museum in the old station building, and it's free to enter. There's also a tea room on the platform. Unfortunately, the riverside path to the village is closed today because of flooding, so please stay near the station.

On the return journey, the buffet car will be open. It serves hot drinks and sandwiches, but it only accepts cash.

If you've enjoyed today, please think about becoming a member. Members get half-price travel and a magazine four times a year. You can pick up a form at the ticket office.

Enjoy the journey.

[Notes]
Engine name: Morning (4) ______
Best view of viaduct: from the (5) ______ side
question: Why did the railway line originally close?
choices: Lorries began to carry the stone instead.
The quarries ran out of stone.
Too few passengers used the trains.
answer: Lorries began to carry the stone instead.
explanation: 1962年にトラックが石の輸送を引き継いだために閉鎖された。

passage:
Hello, and thanks for joining this volunteers' open evening at the Broadmere Steam Railway. I'm Helen Ostrowski, the volunteer manager. Many of you have come because you'd like to drive a steam engine, but I should explain that there's a long path before you get there.

Everyone who works on the engines starts as a cleaner. It's dirty work, and you'll have to arrive very early, often at five in the morning, to help prepare the engine. After a minimum of a year, and a set number of training days, you can apply to become a fireman, which means looking after the fire and the water. Most people spend at least five years as a fireman before they're allowed to train as a driver. So it's a commitment.

However, not all our volunteers work on the trains. In fact, the area where we're most short of help at the moment is not the engines at all, but the track team. These volunteers check and repair the railway line itself. It's outdoor work, mostly done in the winter when trains aren't running.

We also need people in the carriage workshop, where old carriages are restored. Some of them are over a hundred years old, and we need people with woodworking skills especially.

And of course, we always need people at the stations, selling tickets, running the shop and talking to visitors.

All volunteers must be at least sixteen, and for safety reasons, anyone working on the track must be over 18. You'll be given full training, and we provide uniforms and safety boots.

We ask volunteers to commit to at least two days a month. And there's a social club, with a quiz night every month.

[Notes]
Carriage workshop: people with (4) ______ skills especially needed
Minimum age for track work: (5) ______
question: What is the first role for people who want to work on the engines?
choices: cleaner
fireman
driver
explanation: エンジンの仕事をする人は全員まず cleaner から始める。

Hi, this is Sam from the Coldwater Heritage Railway with some news about our special events this winter.

Our most popular event, the Santa Express, runs every weekend in December. Children meet Santa on the train and receive a gift. Last year, tickets sold out within a week, so this year we've added extra trains on the Friday evenings before Christmas. Tickets go on sale on the 1st of October, and must be booked online. We won't be selling them at the station.

The trains will be decorated with lights, and there'll be carol singing by a local school choir. Hot chocolate and mince pies are included in the price for children, while adults can buy mulled juice or coffee at the buffet.

Something new this year is our Winter Wildlife walk. The railway passes through a nature reserve, and on Tuesday mornings in January, a ranger will join the train and lead a walk from Fenwick Halt to spot birds that spend the winter here. Please bring binoculars if you have them, and wear boots, as the path is usually muddy.

For adults, we're also running a dining train on New Year's Eve. It leaves at seven p.m. and returns just after midnight, so passengers can watch the fireworks from the hill. It's quite expensive, but it includes a three-course meal.

Please note that the station car park will be closed from the 2nd to the 10th of January for resurfacing. During that time, visitors should use the car park at the village hall, which is a ten-minute walk away.

And don't forget that we sell gift vouchers, which can be used for any journey or event.

[Notes]
Winter Wildlife walk: on (4) ______ mornings in January
Alternative car park: at the village (5) ______

choices: There are extra trains on Friday evenings.

Children can now travel for free.
answer: There are extra trains on Friday evenings.
explanation: 去年すぐ売り切れたので、クリスマス前の金曜夜に列車を増やした。

passage:
Hi, this is Sam from the Coldwater Heritage Railway with some news about our special events this winter.

Our most popular event, the Santa Express, runs every weekend in December. Children meet Santa on the train and receive a gift. Last year, tickets sold out within a week, so this year we've added extra trains on the Friday evenings before Christmas. Tickets go on sale on the 1st of October, and must be booked online. We won't be selling them at the station.

The trains will be decorated with lights, and there'll be carol singing by a local school choir. Hot chocolate and mince pies are included in the price for children, while adults can buy mulled juice or coffee at the buffet.

Something new this year is our Winter Wildlife walk. The railway passes through a nature reserve, and on Tuesday mornings in January, a ranger will join the train and lead a walk from Fenwick Halt to spot birds that spend the winter here. Please bring binoculars if you have them, and wear boots, as the path is usually muddy.

For adults, we're also running a dining train on New Year's Eve. It leaves at seven p.m. and returns just after midnight, so passengers can watch the fireworks from the hill. It's quite expensive, but it includes a three-course meal.

Please note that the station car park will be closed from the 2nd to the 10th of January for resurfacing. During that time, visitors should use the car park at the village hall, which is a ten-minute walk away.

And don't forget that we sell gift vouchers, which can be used for any journey or event.
